LyTimeT delivers the lowest analytical mean squared error among CNN-based and transformer-only baselines.
LyTimeT remains invariant under background perturbations, demonstrating robustness to nuisance variation.
Lyapunov regularization improves MI, lowers AMSE, and reduces long-horizon error, enhancing stability and interpretability.
LyTimeT-Lite variant maintains near-optimal performance with lower computational cost, suitable for real-time deployment.
future_direction: Incorporating physics-informed priors such as symplectic structures, conservation laws, or energy-preserving constraints.
Investigating hierarchical and sparse attention mechanisms to scale to higher-resolution videos and partially observed systems.
Exploring online or continual learning to adapt latent variables in evolving environments for closed-loop control applications.
papers.abstract: Extracting the true dynamical variables of a system from high-dimensional video is challenging due to distracting visual factors such as background motion, occlusions, and texture changes. We propose LyTimeT, a two-phase framework for interpretable variable extraction that learns robust and stable latent representations of dynamical systems. In Phase 1, LyTimeT employs a spatio-temporal TimeSformer-based autoencoder that uses global attention to focus on dynamically relevant regions while suppressing nuisance variation, enabling distraction-robust latent state learning and accurate long-horizon video prediction. In Phase 2, we probe the learned latent space, select the most physically meaningful dimensions using linear correlation analysis, and refine the transition dynamics with a Lyapunov-based stability regularizer to enforce contraction and reduce error accumulation during roll-outs. Experiments on five synthetic benchmarks and four real-world dynamical systems, including chaotic phenomena, show that LyTimeT achieves mutual information and intrinsic dimension estimates closest to ground truth, remains invariant under background perturbations, and delivers the lowest analytical mean squared error among CNN-based (TIDE) and transformer-only baselines. Our results demonstrate that combining spatio-temporal attention with stability constraints yields predictive models that are not only accurate but also physically interpretable.

papers.title: Representation Learning on a Random Lattice
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a geometric model of data distributions as random lattices, analyzed via percolation theory, and categorizes learned features into context, component, and surface features.
papers.conclusion: The random lattice model provides a geometric perspective on data distributions that is qualitatively consistent with recent mechanistic interpretability findings and suggests directions for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Features can be categorized into context, component, and surface features based on data distribution geometry.
A power-law distribution of useful latent features emerges from the random lattice model.
Sparse dictionary learning methods like SAEs are most useful in subcritical regimes where feature sparsity predominates.
Component features may require multidimensional representations, contrary to the linear representation hypothesis.
The model suggests that SAEs may imperfectly recover true features that have a nested hierarchy, consistent with feature splitting observations.
future_direction: Explore interpretability methods sensitive to finding multidimensional features.
Develop SAE variants with inductive biases for hierarchical structure, such as nested groups of latents.
Develop a richer model with weighted bonds between dataset elements to better capture inexact family resemblances.
papers.abstract: Decomposing a deep neural network's learned representations into interpretable features could greatly enhance its safety and reliability. To better understand features, we adopt a geometric perspective, viewing them as a learned coordinate system for mapping an embedded data distribution. We motivate a model of a generic data distribution as a random lattice and analyze its properties using percolation theory. Learned features are categorized into context, component, and surface features. The model is qualitatively consistent with recent findings in mechanistic interpretability and suggests directions for future research.

papers.title: Multimodal Task Vectors Enable Many-Shot Multimodal In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How to enable Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) to perform many-shot in-context learning without being limited by context length, by compressing examples into implicit representations (task vectors) in the model's attention heads?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Multimodal Task Vectors (MTV), compact implicit representations of in-context examples stored in attention heads, enabling many-shot multimodal in-context learning without fine-tuning and overcoming context length limitations.
papers.conclusion: MTV enables many-shot multimodal in-context learning, scales with examples, and generalizes to similar tasks without requiring fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
MTV outperforms zero-shot and few-shot ICL on various vision-language tasks.
MTV performance scales with the number of compressed examples (shots and iterations).
MTV can be used alongside explicit few-shot examples, freeing up context length.
MTV attention heads extracted on one task can generalize to similar out-of-domain tasks.
papers.limitation:
MTV requires interleaved LMMs and may not work as well on non-interleaved models.
Computing mean activations requires multiple forward passes, which can be computationally expensive.
papers.abstract: The recent success of interleaved Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) in few-shot learning suggests that in-context learning (ICL) with many examples can be promising for learning new tasks. However, this many-shot multimodal ICL setting has one crucial problem: it is fundamentally limited by the model's context length set at pretraining. The problem is especially prominent in the multimodal domain, which processes both text and images, requiring additional tokens. This motivates the need for a multimodal method to compress many shots into fewer tokens without finetuning. In this work, we enable LMMs to perform multimodal, many-shot in-context learning by leveraging Multimodal Task Vectors (MTV) -- compact implicit representations of in-context examples compressed in the model's attention heads. Specifically, we first demonstrate the existence of such MTV in LMMs and then leverage these extracted MTV to enable many-shot in-context learning for various vision-and-language tasks. Our experiments suggest that MTV can scale in performance with the number of compressed shots and generalize to similar out-of-domain tasks without additional context length for inference. Code: https://github.com/Brandon3964/MultiModal-Task-Vector

papers.title: On Privileged and Convergent Bases in Neural Network Representations
papers.research_question: What is the significance of feature directions represented by individual neurons in neural networks, and do networks converge to a unique basis across different training runs?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks do not naturally converge to a unique basis, but freezing early layers can enforce basis convergence, and linear mode connectivity improvements with width are not due to increased basis correlation.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks do not have a privileged basis that is unique across runs, but a convergent basis can be achieved by freezing early layers, which is useful for interpretability and modular training.
papers.key_findings:
perm-corr remains nearly constant across width, indicating no convergence to a unique basis.
LMC barrier decreases with width, but this improvement is not due to increased basis correlation.
Networks cannot learn rotationally invariant representations; random rotations degrade performance.
Freezing early layers increases basis correlation and reduces identity stitching penalty.
Basis correlation is higher when early layers are frozen identically.
papers.abstract: In this study, we investigate whether the representations learned by neural networks possess a privileged and convergent basis. Specifically, we examine the significance of feature directions represented by individual neurons. First, we establish that arbitrary rotations of neural representations cannot be inverted (unlike linear networks), indicating that they do not exhibit complete rotational invariance. Subsequently, we explore the possibility of multiple bases achieving identical performance. To do this, we compare the bases of networks trained with the same parameters but with varying random initializations. Our study reveals two findings: (1) Even in wide networks such as WideResNets, neural networks do not converge to a unique basis; (2) Basis correlation increases significantly when a few early layers of the network are frozen identically. Furthermore, we analyze Linear Mode Connectivity, which has been studied as a measure of basis correlation. Our findings give evidence that while Linear Mode Connectivity improves with increased network width, this improvement is not due to an increase in basis correlation.

papers.title: Deep Hidden Cognition Facilitates Reliable Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: Can the model’s internal activations effectively distinguish between truthful and false branches in CoT reasoning, and can these signals be used to guide more reliable CoT decoding?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a method that leverages the model's internal truthfulness sensitivity, identified via probing attention heads, to train a confidence predictor. This predictor is then used to guide beam search during CoT generation, significantly enhancing the reliability of CoT reasoning by reducing error accumulation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method, which leverages internal truthfulness signals to train a confidence predictor and guide CoT generation, significantly enhances the reliability of CoT reasoning across diverse tasks and models.
papers.key_findings:
The model's internal activations during CoT reasoning encode truthfulness information, which can be extracted via probing attention heads.
A confidence predictor trained on these activations outperforms baselines like sequence likelihood and verbalized confidence in calibration metrics.
Integrating the confidence predictor into a beam search framework for CoT generation improves reasoning accuracy across diverse unimodal and multimodal tasks and model scales.
The method is compatible with self-correction techniques and generalizes to specialized reasoning models like DeepSeek R1.
papers.abstract: Chain of Thought (CoT) reasoning has demonstrated remarkable deep reasoning capabilities in both large language models (LLMs) and multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, its reliability is often undermined by the accumulation of errors in intermediate steps. This paper introduces an novel approach to calibrate the CoT reasoning accuracy by leveraging the model's intrinsic veracity encoding. We discover that specific attention head activations reliably reflect the truthfulness of reasoning steps in CoT. Based on this insight, we train a confidence predictor to evaluate the correctness of each reasoning step using these truthfulness-sensitive activations, dynamically selecting the most plausible reasoning path via beam search. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines (e.g., Few-Shot CoT, Self-Consistency, and Self-Evaluation Guided Beam Search) across the mathematical, symbolic, and commonsense reasoning tasks, exhibiting superior accuracy and reliability in both unimodal and multimodal settings. We further validate the approach on large reasoning models, confirming its applicability to specialized reasoning models. Additionally, we explore the role of the model's self-correction ability in CoT reasoning. This work provides a novel reliability improvement path for CoT reasoning with broad application potential.

papers.title: Mechanistic Independence: A Principle for Identifiable Disentangled Representations
papers.research_question: Under what conditions can disentangled representations be identified without relying on statistical assumptions, by using mechanistic independence criteria?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a unified framework for disentangled representations based on mechanistic independence, proposing several independence criteria and proving identifiability theorems for latent subspaces under nonlinear, non-invertible mixing.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic independence provides a unifying framework that clarifies the conditions for identifiability of disentangled representations without relying on statistical assumptions.
papers.key_findings:
Local disentanglement implies global disentanglement under mild topological conditions (path-connectedness and local injectivity).
Type D independence (disjoint support) yields identifiability of latent subspaces up to block-wise invertible transforms and permutations.
Type M independence (mutual non-inclusion) yields identifiability when combined with a sparsity regularizer.
Type S independence (sparsity gap) yields identifiability even when supports overlap.
Type Hn independence (vanishing cross-derivatives) yields identifiability when the generator is separable of order n.
papers.limitation: The sparsity gap condition (Type S) is intractable to optimize in practice, and finding robust surrogate losses is an open problem.
future_direction: Identifying robust surrogate losses for the sparsity gap condition (Type S).
papers.abstract: Disentangled representations seek to recover latent factors of variation underlying observed data, yet their identifiability is still not fully understood. We introduce a unified framework in which disentanglement is achieved through mechanistic independence, which characterizes latent factors by how they act on observed variables rather than by their latent distribution. This perspective is invariant to changes of the latent density, even when such changes induce statistical dependencies among factors. Within this framework, we propose several related independence criteria -- ranging from support-based and sparsity-based to higher-order conditions -- and show that each yields identifiability of latent subspaces, even under nonlinear, non-invertible mixing. We further establish a hierarchy among these criteria and provide a graph-theoretic characterization of latent subspaces as connected components. Together, these results clarify the conditions under which disentangled representations can be identified without relying on statistical assumptions.

papers.title: Towards a unified and verified understanding of group-operation networks
papers.research_question: How do one-hidden-layer neural networks trained on the binary operation of finite groups compute the group composition, and can a unified and verified explanation be provided?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a unified mechanistic explanation (the ρ-set circuit) for how neural networks compute group operations, and verifies this explanation by translating it into compact formal proofs that lower-bound model accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The ρ-set circuit explanation unifies previous interpretability results on group-operation networks and is quantitatively validated through compact proofs, representing a step towards rigorous evaluation of mechanistic interpretations.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks trained on group composition implement bi-equivariant ρ-set circuits that approximate the group operation.
The model's learned representation decomposes into irreducible group representations (irreps) acting on discrete ρ-sets.
The explanation can be converted into a compact proof that guarantees a lower bound on model accuracy, providing a quantitative evaluation of interpretability.
Previous explanations (coset concentration and irrep sparsity) are incomplete and do not yield non-vacuous accuracy bounds when formalized.
For a significant fraction of models, the ρ-set explanation yields near-perfect accuracy bounds, while for others, deviations (a-bad, ρ-bad) indicate incomplete understanding.
papers.limitation:
The ρ-set explanation does not hold for all trained models; some exhibit deviations where the projection vector a is not constant (a-bad) or the double sum over the ρ-set is incomplete (ρ-bad).
The analysis and compact proof method are primarily demonstrated on symmetric groups (S5, S4) and the alternating group A5; extension to groups with complex irreps is preliminary.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to groups with complex and quaternionic irreducible representations.
Improve the compact proof bounds, particularly for cross-entropy loss.
Investigate the failure modes (a-bad, ρ-bad) to understand how models compute the group operation in those cases.
papers.abstract: A recent line of work in mechanistic interpretability has focused on reverse-engineering the computation performed by neural networks trained on the binary operation of finite groups. We investigate the internals of one-hidden-layer neural networks trained on this task, revealing previously unidentified structure and producing a more complete description of such models in a step towards unifying the explanations of previous works (Chughtai et al., 2023; Stander et al., 2024). Notably, these models approximate equivariance in each input argument. We verify that our explanation applies to a large fraction of networks trained on this task by translating it into a compact proof of model performance, a quantitative evaluation of the extent to which we faithfully and concisely explain model internals. In the main text, we focus on the symmetric group S5. For models trained on this group, our explanation yields a guarantee of model accuracy that runs 3x faster than brute force and gives a >=95% accuracy bound for 45% of the models we trained. We were unable to obtain nontrivial non-vacuous accuracy bounds using only explanations from previous works.

papers.title: Enhancing Pre-trained Representation Classifiability can Boost its Interpretability
papers.research_question: Can classifiability-oriented pre-trained representations achieve high interpretability and classifiability simultaneously?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers a positive correlation between interpretability and classifiability in pre-trained vision representations, introduces the Inherent Interpretability Score (IIS) to quantify representation interpretability, and shows that improving one can mutually promote the other.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability and classifiability are mutually promoting for classifiability-oriented pre-trained representations, allowing practitioners to unify improvements in both aspects for vision models.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability and classifiability of pre-trained representations are positively correlated, not conflicting.
Representations with higher classifiability contain more interpretable semantics that can be captured in interpretations.
Fine-tuning pre-trained models with an interpretability maximization objective (simplified IIS) can further improve their classifiability on downstream tasks.
Predictions based on the interpretations of high-classifiability representations suffer less accuracy degradation compared to the original representations.
The mutual promoting relationship provides a new pathway for interpretable representation learning.
papers.limitation:
Investigations of the underlying mechanism leading to the positive correlation between interpretability and classifiability have not been conducted.
The method fine-tunes representations by maximizing a simplified version of IIS, not the original IIS.
future_direction: Investigate the underlying mechanisms of the observed positive correlation between interpretability and classifiability.
Better integrate the Inherent Interpretability Score (IIS) into the training process of pre-trained models.
papers.abstract: The visual representation of a pre-trained model prioritizes the classifiability on downstream tasks, while the widespread applications for pre-trained visual models have posed new requirements for representation interpretability. However, it remains unclear whether the pre-trained representations can achieve high interpretability and classifiability simultaneously. To answer this question, we quantify the representation interpretability by leveraging its correlation with the ratio of interpretable semantics within the representations. Given the pre-trained representations, only the interpretable semantics can be captured by interpretations, whereas the uninterpretable part leads to information loss. Based on this fact, we propose the Inherent Interpretability Score (IIS) that evaluates the information loss, measures the ratio of interpretable semantics, and quantifies the representation interpretability. In the evaluation of the representation interpretability with different classifiability, we surprisingly discover that the interpretability and classifiability are positively correlated, i.e., representations with higher classifiability provide more interpretable semantics that can be captured in the interpretations. This observation further supports two benefits to the pre-trained representations. First, the classifiability of representations can be further improved by fine-tuning with interpretability maximization. Second, with the classifiability improvement for the representations, we obtain predictions based on their interpretations with less accuracy degradation. The discovered positive correlation and corresponding applications show that practitioners can unify the improvements in interpretability and classifiability for pre-trained vision models. Codes are available at https://github.com/ssfgunner/IIS.

papers.title: Neurons to Words: A Novel Method for Automated Neural Network Interpretability and Alignment
papers.research_question: Can neural network activations be automatically translated into human-readable language to interpret the internal workings of the model?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a generic, scalable method for automatically interpreting neural networks by translating activations into human-readable language, demonstrated on a CNN trained on MNIST.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates the feasibility of automatically interpreting neural networks by converting activations into human-readable language, and suggests that with sufficient computational resources, the method could scale to monitor the internal mechanisms of advanced AI models.
papers.key_findings:
The method successfully translates activations of a CNN's first convolutional layer into human-readable descriptions of shapes.
Fine-tuned LLMs (Mistral7b and Mixtral8x7b) achieve high accuracy in identifying shapes from synthetic and MNIST data.
The interpreter models can generalize to unseen shapes (e.g., curves) by leveraging learned features and pre-trained knowledge.
The method loses some spatial information and granularity due to flattening and binning of activations.
Larger and more diverse datasets could improve performance and generalization.
papers.limitation:
The method loses spatial information and granularity due to flattening and binning of activations.
The 28x28 image resolution makes it hard to distinguish between round shapes and angular corners.
The structured descriptions lack linguistic diversity, making the model less flexible in generating natural language.
The fine-tuned model sometimes continues generating activations or shapes even after accurate predictions.
Computational resources limited the study to the MNIST dataset.
future_direction: Using larger and more detailed datasets to yield more informative activations.
Leveraging LLMs for natural description generation to improve linguistic diversity.
Training multiple interpreters in parallel to improve consistency and comprehensiveness.
papers.abstract: Recent years have witnessed an increase in the parameter size of frontier AI models by multiple orders of magnitude. This trend is driven by empirical observations, known as scaling laws, which show that model performance scales with model size, dataset size, and computational power. Motivated by this, researchers are training ever-larger models in pursuit of unlocking new capabilities. However, the growing complexity of these models makes understanding their inner workings increasingly challenging. Interpretability is crucial not only in fields like medicine and biotechnology, where understanding the internals of these models could lead to new insights but also in super alignment, where it is the goal to ensure that AI is aligned and acts according to human values and interests. We present a generic, scalable first-of-its-kind method for automatically interpreting neural networks. In a proof-of-concept study we establish the viability of converting neural network activations - here for the first layer of a Convolutional Neural Network - into human-readable language. Additionally, we propose modifications to scale this method for understanding neural networks of any size. In anticipation of more capable large language models, this method could enable the monitoring of their internal mechanisms and decisions.

papers.title: Concept Algebra for (Score-Based) Text-Controlled Generative Models
papers.research_question: How are concepts represented and can they be manipulated in text-controlled generative models? The paper investigates whether concepts correspond to subspaces of a representation space and develops a method to identify and edit these subspaces.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a mathematical framework showing that concepts correspond to subspaces of the score representation in text-controlled generative models, and develops 'concept algebra' to manipulate concepts by projecting onto these subspaces.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that concepts align with subspaces of the score representation, enabling precise manipulation of concepts in diffusion models through linear-algebraic operations.
papers.key_findings:
Many binary concepts (e.g., dog vs. cat) correspond to subspaces and can be manipulated with concept algebra.
Concept algebra is more effective at disentangling hard-to-separate concepts (e.g., content and style) compared to direct prompting or concept composition.
Concept algebra can sample from mixture distributions over concepts, such as generating a mix of genders for 'a portrait of a mathematician'.
Edits to the concept subspace that do not correspond to any English prompt (e.g., an arithmetic mean of male and female) still affect the concept appropriately, producing androgynous figures.
Concept algebra can manipulate abstract concepts like 'subject' to improve fine-tuning, e.g., by masking out background information to generate a specific toy in front of the Eiffel Tower without background interference.
papers.limitation:
The method requires causal separability between concepts, which may not hold for interacting concepts (e.g., sex and species).
Manipulating entire score functions is computationally burdensome.
future_direction: Develop more efficient procedures for manipulating concepts, possibly by moving from score manipulation to bottleneck layer manipulation.
Explore the connection between the score-representation view and manipulation of the bottleneck layer in UNet.
papers.abstract: This paper concerns the structure of learned representations in text-guided generative models, focusing on score-based models. A key property of such models is that they can compose disparate concepts in a `disentangled' manner. This suggests these models have internal representations that encode concepts in a `disentangled' manner. Here, we focus on the idea that concepts are encoded as subspaces of some representation space. We formalize what this means, show there's a natural choice for the representation, and develop a simple method for identifying the part of the representation corresponding to a given concept. In particular, this allows us to manipulate the concepts expressed by the model through algebraic manipulation of the representation. We demonstrate the idea with examples using Stable Diffusion. Code in https://github.com/zihao12/concept-algebra-code

papers.title: Intermediate Entity-based Sparse Interpretable Representation Learning
papers.research_question: Can we maintain the interpretable semantics afforded by Interpretable Entity Representations (IERs) while improving predictive performance on downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ItsIRL, an extension to IERs that adds a decoder network which can be fine-tuned for downstream tasks, improving performance while maintaining the interpretability of the intermediate entity type layer.
papers.conclusion: ItsIRL provides an interpretable model that can be fine-tuned for improved performance and allows for model debugging via entity type manipulation and global explainability through class prototypes.
papers.key_findings:
ItsIRL outperforms prior IER methods on biomedical benchmark tasks.
Pre-training the decoder network is important for task performance.
Counterfactual manipulation of the intermediate entity type layer can be used to debug and improve model predictions.
Class prototypes constructed from entity type representations reveal global semantic properties learned by the model.
Using coarse, noisy entity type sets for manipulation allows ItsIRL to achieve performance comparable to dense, non-interpretable models.
papers.limitation: The entity type sets used for counterfactual manipulation are coarse and noisy, and their quality affects the manipulation results.
future_direction: Determining the best entity type manipulation method for each error case could be done by observing performance on a holdout set.
Having experts edit or choose better terms to form type sets associated with each class would improve performance.
papers.abstract: Interpretable entity representations (IERs) are sparse embeddings that are "human-readable" in that dimensions correspond to fine-grained entity types and values are predicted probabilities that a given entity is of the corresponding type. These methods perform well in zero-shot and low supervision settings. Compared to standard dense neural embeddings, such interpretable representations may permit analysis and debugging. However, while fine-tuning sparse, interpretable representations improves accuracy on downstream tasks, it destroys the semantics of the dimensions which were enforced in pre-training. Can we maintain the interpretable semantics afforded by IERs while improving predictive performance on downstream tasks? Toward this end, we propose Intermediate enTity-based Sparse Interpretable Representation Learning (ItsIRL). ItsIRL realizes improved performance over prior IERs on biomedical tasks, while maintaining "interpretability" generally and their ability to support model debugging specifically. The latter is enabled in part by the ability to perform "counterfactual" fine-grained entity type manipulation, which we explore in this work. Finally, we propose a method to construct entity type based class prototypes for revealing global semantic properties of classes learned by our model.

papers.title: Identifying Sub-networks in Neural Networks via Functionally Similar Representations
papers.research_question: Is it possible to detect how many distinct (complex) functions exist in a learned network, and which layers correspond to each such function?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes using Gromov-Wasserstein distance to automatically identify functionally similar layers and subnetworks in neural networks, providing insights into model behavior and aiding in tasks like model compression and fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: GW distance provides an automatic, low-cost approach to identify subnetworks in neural networks, revealing functional abstractions and facilitating applications like model compression and efficient fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
GW distance can identify functionally similar layers and reveal block structures in neural networks, as shown in synthetic, NLP, and vision tasks.
In synthetic tasks with layer-wise training, GW distance aligns with known functional divisions (e.g., three groups corresponding to three modular sum functions).
In fine-tuned BERT models, GW distance shows distinct subnetwork blocks (e.g., early vs. late layers) that correlate with performance and training dynamics.
The method can track the emergence of subnetworks during training, showing a rapid increase in GW distance coinciding with performance improvements (grokking-like behavior).
In ResNet9 on CIFAR-10, GW distance reveals meaningful subnetwork structures aligned with feature learning stages.
papers.limitation:
Requires access to intermediate layer representations, which may not be available for some black-box models.
Assumes the proposed distances correctly represent the functional similarities.
Findings are limited to the datasets and models studied and are not guaranteed to be observed in other scenarios.
future_direction: Investigate larger models to observe general trends and applications of functional similarity.
Theoretical study of special properties of GW distances within the context of neural network interpretability.
papers.abstract: Providing human-understandable insights into the inner workings of neural networks is an important step toward achieving more explainable and trustworthy AI. Existing approaches to such mechanistic interpretability typically require substantial prior knowledge and manual effort, with strategies tailored to specific tasks. In this work, we take a step toward automating the understanding of the network by investigating the existence of distinct sub-networks. Specifically, we explore a novel automated and task-agnostic approach based on the notion of functionally similar representations within neural networks to identify similar and dissimilar layers, revealing potential sub-networks. We achieve this by proposing, for the first time to our knowledge, the use of Gromov-Wasserstein distance, which overcomes challenges posed by varying distributions and dimensionalities across intermediate representations, issues that complicate direct layer to layer comparisons. On algebraic, language, and vision tasks, we observe the emergence of sub-groups within neural network layers corresponding to functional abstractions. Through downstream applications of model compression and fine-tuning, we show the proposed approach offers meaningful insights into the behavior of neural networks with minimal human and computational cost.

papers.title: Just Say No to Single Embeddings: Why Your AI Needs Multiple Perspectives
papers.research_question: How does BERT represent linguistic features internally, and what is the geometric structure of these representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT represents linguistic features in separate semantic and syntactic subspaces, provides evidence of fine-grained geometric representation of word senses, and gives a mathematical argument for the squared-distance tree embedding.
papers.conclusion: The paper's experiments suggest that BERT's internal geometry consists of multiple linear subspaces for different syntactic and semantic information, and that understanding this geometry can help improve transformer architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Attention matrices encode syntactic dependency relations, as shown by linear probes achieving high accuracy.
Parse tree embeddings in BERT approximate Pythagorean embeddings (squared Euclidean distance corresponds to tree distance), and there is a mathematical justification for this.
Word senses are represented as clusters in embedding space, and a simple nearest-neighbor classifier on BERT embeddings achieves state-of-the-art word sense disambiguation.
Semantic information can be isolated in a lower-dimensional subspace via a learned linear transformation (semantic probe).
Concatenating sentences with different word senses can cause embeddings to shift towards the opposing sense, indicating that tokens absorb meaning from all neighboring tokens.
future_direction: Investigating other meaningful subspaces in BERT's internal geometry
Using internal geometry to improve or refine transformer architectures
papers.abstract: Note: This is a work in progress document We present empirical evidence that conversations exhibit consistent geometric signatures when projected into different embedding spaces, alongside surprising variability in local feature detection. Analyzing 229 multi-agent AI dialogues from our prior study on social dynamics [Garcia, 2025], we examine whether geometric properties of conversational trajectories remain consistent across 5 fundamentally different embedding models. Our analysis reveals a striking dichotomy: while global geometric patterns (distance matrices, trajectory shapes) show remarkable consistency across both transformer-based and classical embeddings (correlations ranging from 0.521 to 0.957), local phase detection exhibits extreme variability (F1 scores from 0.08 to 0.36, agreement correlations from -0.14 to 0.76). This pattern of high global consistency with low local agreement suggests that different embedding models may capture distinct projections of conversations existing in a higher-dimensional semantic space. Transport-based analysis supports this interpretation, showing threefold increases in cross-paradigm distances compared to within-paradigm distances. These findings establish that while geometric analysis of conversation captures genuine structural properties, the global-local dichotomy implies fundamental limits on fine-grained analysis and raises intriguing questions about the true dimensionality of conversational dynamics.

papers.title: On the definition and importance of interpretability in scientific machine learning
papers.research_question: What is interpretability in the context of scientific machine learning, and how does interpretability advance scientific knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a definition of interpretability for scientific machine learning that emphasizes understanding of the mechanism over mathematical sparsity, and questions the possibility of interpretable scientific discovery when prior knowledge is lacking.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes by proposing a definition of interpretability focused on physical meaning, and argues that interpretability is useful in science as a tool for unification, with sparsity facilitating derivation from fundamental principles.
papers.key_findings:
Researchers in equation discovery and symbolic regression tend to conflate the concept of sparsity with interpretability.
Existing definitions and methods from the broader interpretable ML literature are inadequate for scientific machine learning.
Interpretability in science should be defined as understanding the physical meaning or mechanism of an equation, not merely its mathematical sparsity.
Sparsity is neither necessary nor sufficient for interpretability in science; prior knowledge is required to connect sparse equations to underlying principles.
Interpretability advances scientific knowledge by unifying disparate phenomena under a small set of fundamental physical principles.
future_direction: Future work will explore whether interpretations can be extracted from recovered equations when relevant prior knowledge is lacking.
papers.abstract: Though neural networks trained on large datasets have been successfully used to describe and predict many physical phenomena, there is a sense among scientists that, unlike traditional scientific models comprising simple mathematical expressions, their findings cannot be integrated into the body of scientific knowledge. Critics of machine learning's inability to produce human-understandable relationships have converged on the concept of "interpretability" as its point of departure from more traditional forms of science. As the growing interest in interpretability has shown, researchers in the physical sciences seek not just predictive models, but also to uncover the fundamental principles that govern a system of interest. However, clarity around a definition of interpretability and the precise role that it plays in science is lacking in the literature. In this work, we argue that researchers in equation discovery and symbolic regression tend to conflate the concept of sparsity with interpretability. We review key papers on interpretable machine learning from outside the scientific community and argue that, though the definitions and methods they propose can inform questions of interpretability for scientific machine learning (SciML), they are inadequate for this new purpose. Noting these deficiencies, we propose an operational definition of interpretability for the physical sciences. Our notion of interpretability emphasizes understanding of the mechanism over mathematical sparsity. Innocuous though it may seem, this emphasis on mechanism shows that sparsity is often unnecessary. It also questions the possibility of interpretable scientific discovery when prior knowledge is lacking. We believe a precise and philosophically informed definition of interpretability in SciML will help focus research efforts toward the most significant obstacles to realizing a data-driven scientific future.

papers.title: Same Task, Different Circuits: Disentangling Modality-Specific Mechanisms in VLMs
papers.research_question: Why do Vision-Language models (VLMs) perform worse on visual tasks compared to analogous textual tasks?
papers.core_contribution: VLMs use largely disjoint circuits for visual and textual tasks, but the functional difference lies in data processing; patching visual token embeddings from later layers to earlier layers (back-patching) reduces the performance gap without training.
papers.conclusion: The performance gap in VLMs arises from disjoint circuits for different modalities, and back-patching provides a training-free method to reduce it by aligning visual representations earlier.
papers.key_findings:
Vision and language circuits are structurally disjoint but implement similar functionalities for query and generation.
The performance gap stems from differences in processing modality-specific data tokens.
Visual token representations become aligned with textual counterparts only in later layers.
Back-patching visual token embeddings from later to earlier layers improves visual task accuracy, closing about a third of the performance gap on average.
The intervention is effective across multiple models and tasks.
papers.limitation:
Focused on single-image question-answering tasks with single-token completions.
Current open models struggle with complex visual reasoning, limiting analysis.
Circuit analysis methods are limited to single-token completions.
Back-patching closes only 32% of the performance gap; causes for the remaining gap are unclear.
Analysis is limited to adapter-based VLMs; may not apply to other fusion approaches.
future_direction: Explore multi-image scenarios, different prompt orders, and more complex visual reasoning tasks.
Investigate varied computational resources per token, especially for visual inputs.
Extend analysis to VLMs with different fusion approaches.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language models (VLMs) show impressive abilities to answer questions on visual inputs (e.g., counting objects in an image), yet demonstrate higher accuracies when performing an analogous task on text (e.g., counting words in a text). We investigate this accuracy gap by identifying and comparing the \textit{circuits} - the task-specific computational sub-graphs - in different modalities. We show that while circuits are largely disjoint between modalities, they implement relatively similar functionalities: the differences lie primarily in processing modality-specific data positions (an image or a text sequence). Zooming in on the image data representations, we observe they become aligned with the higher-performing analogous textual representations only towards later layers, too late in processing to effectively influence subsequent positions. To overcome this, we patch the representations of visual data tokens from later layers back into earlier layers. In experiments with multiple tasks and models, this simple intervention closes a third of the performance gap between the modalities, on average. Our analysis sheds light on the multi-modal performance gap in VLMs and suggests a training-free approach for reducing it.

papers.title: Open Sesame: Getting inside BERT’s Linguistic Knowledge
papers.research_question: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information?
papers.core_contribution: BERT encodes positional information in lower layers and switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. The paper also introduces a 'confusion score' to quantify intrusion effects in BERT's self-attention mechanism.
papers.conclusion: BERT composes increasingly abstract hierarchical representations of linguistic structure using self-attention, but does not show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure found in human processing.
papers.key_findings:
Diagnostic classifiers show BERT's lower layers encode positional information well, while higher layers encode hierarchical information.
The proposed confusion score reveals BERT's attention is sensitive to syntactic structure and grammatical features (number, gender) in subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora.
BERT's attention is not perfectly syntactic; it sometimes attends to grammatically inaccessible or mismatched distractors.
Confusion scores decrease with layer depth, and there is an increase in confusion at layer 4, coinciding with the degradation of positional information.
BERT's performance on possessive constructions in the subject noun task is poor, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
papers.limitation:
BERT performed poorly on possessive constructions in the subject noun task, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
BERT's attention is only incompletely modulated by structural and featural properties, and attention is sometimes spread across grammatically irrelevant elements.
future_direction: Investigate or visualize layer-on-layer changes in BERT’s structural and positional information, particularly between layers 3 and 4.
Retrieve the increasingly hierarchical representations of BERT across layers via the self-attention mechanism.
papers.abstract: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information? Recent work has shown that contextual representations like BERT perform well on tasks that require sensitivity to linguistic structure. We present here two studies which aim to provide a better understanding of the nature of BERT's representations. The first of these focuses on the identification of structurally-defined elements using diagnostic classifiers, while the second explores BERT's representation of subject-verb agreement and anaphor-antecedent dependencies through a quantitative assessment of self-attention vectors. In both cases, we find that BERT encodes positional information about word tokens well on its lower layers, but switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. We conclude then that BERT's representations do indeed model linguistically relevant aspects of hierarchical structure, though they do not appear to show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure that is found in human processing of reflexive anaphora.

papers.title: Transport and Merge: Cross-Architecture Merging for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can we enable high-resource to low-resource knowledge transfer across heterogeneous model architectures through direct model merging?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes an optimal transport-based cross-architecture merging framework that aligns activations to infer neuron correspondences and enables direct weight-space fusion, facilitating knowledge transfer from high-resource to low-resource models.
papers.conclusion: The proposed OT-based framework enables effective cross-architecture model merging, improving target models using only a small calibration set, and provides a practical alternative to distillation when architectures differ.
papers.key_findings:
The method consistently improves performance on low-resource language benchmarks (Malay, Indonesian, Cantonese, Thai).
It also improves domain-specific performance in finance and medical domains.
The method is robust to different source model backbones (e.g., LLaMA3-8B and Qwen2.5-7B).
Fusion does not degrade general capabilities of the target model.
Optimal transport plans reveal sparse neuron-level correspondences between heterogeneous models.
papers.limitation:
May propagate biases, factual errors, or unsafe behaviors from the source model.
Sensitivity to the choice of calibration set; mismatched data can lead to noisy correspondences.
Fusion may fail if the target model lacks sufficient capacity to absorb transferred knowledge.
future_direction: Incorporating safety-aware objectives directly into the transport formulation.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong capabilities by scaling model capacity and training data, yet many real-world deployments rely on smaller models trained or adapted from low-resource data. This gap motivates the need for mechanisms to transfer knowledge from large, high-resource models to smaller, low-resource targets. While model merging provides an effective transfer mechanism, most existing approaches assume architecture-compatible models and therefore cannot directly transfer knowledge from large high-resource LLMs to heterogeneous low-resource targets. In this work, we propose a cross-architecture merging framework based on optimal transport (OT) that aligns activations to infer cross-neuron correspondences between heterogeneous models. The resulting transport plans are then used to guide direct weight-space fusion, enabling effective high-resource to low-resource transfer using only a small set of inputs. Extensive experiments across low-resource languages and specialized domains demonstrate consistent improvements over target models.

papers.title: Convergent Learning: Do different neural networks learn the same representations?
papers.research_question: Do different neural networks with the same architecture trained from different random initializations learn the same representations (i.e., exhibit convergent learning)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces methods to compare neural network representations and shows that networks exhibit partial convergent learning, with some features learned reliably across networks and others not, and that representations are a mix of local and slightly distributed codes.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks exhibit convergent learning to some extent, and the introduced methods are effective for understanding and comparing the representations they learn.
papers.key_findings:
Some features are learned reliably in multiple networks, yet other features are not consistently learned.
Units learn to span low-dimensional subspaces and, while these subspaces are common to multiple networks, the specific basis vectors learned are not.
The representation codes show evidence of being a mix between a local (single unit) code and slightly, but not fully, distributed codes across multiple units.
The average activation values of neurons vary considerably within a network, yet the mean activation values across different networks converge to an almost identical distribution.
Features learned in different networks are most convergent on the first convolutional layer (conv1) and least convergent on the fourth (conv4).
papers.limitation: Mapping layers for higher layers (conv3-conv5) showed poor performance, and the reasons are not fully understood.
future_direction: Investigate different architectures, training algorithms, and hyperparameters.
Train more powerful predictive models for higher layers with different hyperparameters or architectures.
papers.abstract: Recent success in training deep neural networks have prompted active investigation into the features learned on their intermediate layers. Such research is difficult because it requires making sense of non-linear computations performed by millions of parameters, but valuable because it increases our ability to understand current models and create improved versions of them. In this paper we investigate the extent to which neural networks exhibit what we call convergent learning, which is when the representations learned by multiple nets converge to a set of features which are either individually similar between networks or where subsets of features span similar low-dimensional spaces. We propose a specific method of probing representations: training multiple networks and then comparing and contrasting their individual, learned representations at the level of neurons or groups of neurons. We begin research into this question using three techniques to approximately align different neural networks on a feature level: a bipartite matching approach that makes one-to-one assignments between neurons, a sparse prediction approach that finds one-to-many mappings, and a spectral clustering approach that finds many-to-many mappings. This initial investigation reveals a few previously unknown properties of neural networks, and we argue that future research into the question of convergent learning will yield many more. The insights described here include (1) that some features are learned reliably in multiple networks, yet other features are not consistently learned; (2) that units learn to span low-dimensional subspaces and, while these subspaces are common to multiple networks, the specific basis vectors learned are not; (3) that the representation codes show evidence of being a mix between a local code and slightly, but not fully, distributed codes across multiple units.

papers.title: Neural Basis Models for Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we scale Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) to large datasets while maintaining interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Neural Basis Models (NBM), a new subfamily of Generalized Additive Models that uses basis decomposition of shape functions to achieve scalability and interpretability on large datasets.
papers.conclusion: Neural Basis Models address scalability and performance issues of GAMs while preserving interpretability, and can be used as drop-in replacements for black-box deep neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
NBMs achieve state-of-the-art performance among GAMs, with 5x-50x fewer parameters and 4x-7x higher throughput than Neural Additive Models (NAM).
NBMs scale to high-dimensional sparse datasets where other GAMs fail, and are more stable in terms of shape function consistency across training runs.
Pairwise interactions via NB2M can match or exceed the performance of black-box models like MLPs on many datasets.
NBMs can be extended to model pairwise interactions with linear parameter growth, unlike quadratic growth in NA2Ms.
The number of basis functions needed is small (B=100 for NBM, B=200 for NB2M) and the model is not overly sensitive to this choice.
papers.limitation: The approach has limitations with respect to the number of features; beyond 10,000 dense or 1 million sparse features, feature selection is needed to scale further.
future_direction: Explore visual interpretability by applying NBMs directly to pixel space or learning visual features with lower order interactions.
Use more interpretable basis functions, such as polynomials, for higher order interactions.
Apply feature selection algorithms to scale to even larger numbers of features.
papers.abstract: Due to the widespread use of complex machine learning models in real-world applications, it is becoming critical to explain model predictions. However, these models are typically black-box deep neural networks, explained post-hoc via methods with known faithfulness limitations. Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) are an inherently interpretable class of models that address this limitation by learning a non-linear shape function for each feature separately, followed by a linear model on top. However, these models are typically difficult to train, require numerous parameters, and are difficult to scale. We propose an entirely new subfamily of GAMs that utilizes basis decomposition of shape functions. A small number of basis functions are shared among all features, and are learned jointly for a given task, thus making our model scale much better to large-scale data with high-dimensional features, especially when features are sparse. We propose an architecture denoted as the Neural Basis Model (NBM) which uses a single neural network to learn these bases. On a variety of tabular and image datasets, we demonstrate that for interpretable machine learning, NBMs are the state-of-the-art in accuracy, model size, and, throughput and can easily model all higher-order feature interactions. Source code is available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/nbm-spam.

papers.title: Understanding Interpretability by generalized distillation in Supervised Classification
papers.research_question: How can interpretability be defined and quantified from an information-theoretic perspective, decoupled from human understanding, using a distillation-like framework?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an information-theoretic framework for interpretability based on distillation, decoupling interpretability from human understanding and providing theoretical bounds for Piece-Wise Linear Neural Networks.
papers.conclusion: The interpretation-by-distillation framework provides a novel interpretability definition from an information-theoretic perspective, with theoretical bounds for ReLU networks, and demonstrates stability and conformity to human understanding.
papers.key_findings:
The interpretability measure conforms to human understanding when explaining predictions of InceptionV3 on Stanford40, with higher interpretability when cropped images contain relevant objects.
Ensembles of simpler models (e.g., SVM, Decision Tree, Logistic Regression) can interpret complex models like MiniVGGNet with high interpretability.
Interpretability converges as the number of query points increases, demonstrating stability of the empirical interpretation.
The interpretability formulation is decoupled from accuracy, as shown by Decision Tree having higher accuracy but lower interpretability on MNIST compared to Fashion-MNIST.
The framework exhibits double ascent behavior in interpretability, aligning with modern deep learning phenomena.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical interpretability estimates are far from empirical estimates due to exponential complexity bounds.
Model entropy definition only considers arrangement of decision boundary, not shape.
Theoretical bounds are limited to Piece-Wise Linear Networks (PWLNs).
future_direction: Explore the effect of dataset complexity on interpretability.
Incorporate the shape of the decision boundary into the entropy definition.
Extend the theoretical bounds to other networks like CNNs when their complexities are defined.
papers.abstract: The ability to interpret decisions taken by Machine Learning (ML) models is fundamental to encourage trust and reliability in different practical applications. Recent interpretation strategies focus on human understanding of the underlying decision mechanisms of the complex ML models. However, these strategies are restricted by the subjective biases of humans. To dissociate from such human biases, we propose an interpretation-by-distillation formulation that is defined relative to other ML models. We generalize the distillation technique for quantifying interpretability, using an information-theoretic perspective, removing the role of ground-truth from the definition of interpretability. Our work defines the entropy of supervised classification models, providing bounds on the entropy of Piece-Wise Linear Neural Networks (PWLNs), along with the first theoretical bounds on the interpretability of PWLNs. We evaluate our proposed framework on the MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and Stanford40 datasets and demonstrate the applicability of the proposed theoretical framework in different supervised classification scenarios.

papers.title: Decoding Dark Matter: Specialized Sparse Autoencoders for Interpreting Rare Concepts in Foundation Models
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently capture rare, subdomain-specific concepts in foundation models using sparse autoencoders, without simply scaling the SAE width?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Specialized Sparse Autoencoders (SSAEs) for capturing rare, subdomain-specific concepts in foundation models, and demonstrates their effectiveness in capturing tail concepts and improving bias mitigation.
papers.conclusion: SSAEs provide a powerful new lens for interpreting foundation models in subdomains, effectively capturing rare concepts and offering practical utility in tasks such as bias mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
SSAEs capture a greater proportion of tail concepts than standard SAEs trained on general-purpose data.
Dense retrieval is an effective data selection strategy for training SSAEs, outperforming sparse retrieval (BM25).
Tilted Empirical Risk Minimization (TERM) improves concept recall in SAEs, especially for rare concepts, at the cost of some precision.
In a case study on the Bias in Bios dataset, SSAEs achieve a 12.5% increase in worst-group classification accuracy when used to remove spurious gender information.
TERM-trained SAEs exhibit stronger activations and lower entropy for tail concepts, making them suitable for rare concept detection.
papers.limitation:
SSAEs require a small seed concept dataset to begin the data selection process.
TERM prioritizes recall, sacrificing some control (precision) for broader concept coverage.
future_direction: Extending SSAEs to other domains and modalities
Applying SSAEs to real-world safety-critical systems
papers.abstract: Understanding and mitigating the potential risks associated with foundation models (FMs) hinges on developing effective interpretability methods. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising tool for disentangling FM representations, but they struggle to capture rare, yet crucial concepts in the data. We introduce Specialized Sparse Autoencoders (SSAEs), designed to illuminate these elusive dark matter features by focusing on specific subdomains. We present a practical recipe for training SSAEs, demonstrating the efficacy of dense retrieval for data selection and the benefits of Tilted Empirical Risk Minimization as a training objective to improve concept recall. Our evaluation of SSAEs on standard metrics, such as downstream perplexity and $L_0$ sparsity, show that they effectively capture subdomain tail concepts, exceeding the capabilities of general-purpose SAEs. We showcase the practical utility of SSAEs in a case study on the Bias in Bios dataset, where SSAEs achieve a 12.5\% increase in worst-group classification accuracy when applied to remove spurious gender information. SSAEs provide a powerful new lens for peering into the inner workings of FMs in subdomains.

papers.title: From Bias to Balance: Exploring and Mitigating Spatial Bias in LVLMs
papers.research_question: What is the spatial bias in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) and how does it affect their semantic understanding when identical visual information is placed at different locations within an image?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies that spatial bias in LVLMs stems from a mismatch between vision encoder and LLM attention mechanisms, and proposes Adaptive Global Context Injection (AGCI) to mitigate this bias by injecting global visual context into image tokens.
papers.conclusion: Spatial bias in LVLMs is caused by the disruption of global information flow due to causal attention, and AGCI effectively mitigates this bias without architectural changes.
papers.key_findings:
LVLMs exhibit significant spatial bias, with predictions varying when key visual content is placed at different locations.
The bias originates from the loss of global image context due to causal attention in LLMs, not from the vision encoder.
AGCI improves spatial robustness and average accuracy on probing tasks across multiple LVLMs.
AGCI also enhances performance on downstream tasks including science QA, hallucination benchmarks, and text VQA.
Larger models also show spatial bias, and AGCI is effective for them as well.
papers.limitation:
The probing experiments focus on a 3x3 spatial grid, which may not capture more fine-grained or irregular spatial variations.
Due to computational constraints, the evaluation does not include very large models such as Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B.
future_direction: Investigating whether spatial bias persists or evolves in larger-scale models.
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of multimodal tasks, yet their robustness to spatial variations remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we present a systematic study of the spatial bias of LVLMs, focusing on how models respond when identical key visual information is placed at different locations within an image. Through a carefully designed probing dataset, we demonstrate that current LVLMs often produce inconsistent outputs under such spatial shifts, revealing a fundamental limitation in their spatial-semantic understanding. Further analysis shows that this phenomenon originates not from the vision encoder, which reliably perceives and interprets visual content across positions, but from the unbalanced design of position embeddings in the language model component. In particular, the widely adopted position embedding strategies, such as RoPE, introduce imbalance during cross-modal interaction, leading image tokens at different positions to exert unequal influence on semantic understanding. To mitigate this issue, we introduce Balanced Position Assignment (BaPA), a simple yet effective mechanism that assigns identical position embeddings to all image tokens, promoting a more balanced integration of visual information. Extensive experiments show that BaPA enhances the spatial robustness of LVLMs without retraining and further boosts their performance across diverse multimodal benchmarks when combined with lightweight fine-tuning. Further analysis of information flow reveals that BaPA yields balanced attention, enabling more holistic visual understanding.

papers.title: Interpretability as Alignment: Making Internal Understanding a Design Principle
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic interpretability be reframed as a design principle to provide verifiable causal evidence for private AI governance mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reframes mechanistic interpretability as a design principle for AI governance, proposing interpretability-first architectures to provide verifiable causal evidence for private oversight mechanisms like audits and certification.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability is essential for AI safety and governance, requiring a combined approach with behavioral methods to ensure models are understandable and aligned.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic interpretability provides verifiable causal evidence necessary for private AI governance mechanisms such as audits and certification.
Interpretability should be embedded as a design constraint in model architectures with features like modularity and audit hooks, rather than applied post-hoc.
Current interpretability methods face limitations including polysemanticity, scalability issues, and epistemic concerns like explanation theater.
Hybrid approaches combining mechanistic interpretability with behavioral methods like RLHF can enhance alignment by providing causal guarantees.
Governance-ready AI requires interpretability-first design to enable accountability and compliance with regulatory frameworks.
papers.limitation:
Polysemantic neurons and entangled features complicate semantic interpretation and regulatory compliance.
Post-hoc interpretability methods are unstable and manipulable, risking 'explanation theater' that undermines audit compliance.
Lack of standardized benchmarks for explanation quality and causal validation weakens audit evidence.
Compute- and expert-intensive nature of mechanistic interpretability limits accessibility and scalability.
Conceptual mismatch between human symbolic explanations and model subsymbolic representations challenges interpretability.
future_direction: Developing auditable interpretability pipelines for generating and validating assurance evidence.
Extending benchmarks like MIB to governance-relevant tasks and developing prototype models with modularity and audit hooks.
Building open-source audit toolchains and piloting circuit-level audits with regulators.
papers.abstract: Frontier AI systems require governance mechanisms that can verify internal alignment, not just behavioral compliance. Private governance mechanisms audits, certification, insurance, and procurement are emerging to complement public regulation, but they require technical substrates that generate verifiable causal evidence about model behavior. This paper argues that mechanistic interpretability provides this substrate. We frame interpretability not as post-hoc explanation but as a design constraint embedding auditability, provenance, and bounded transparency within model architectures. Integrating causal abstraction theory and empirical benchmarks such as MIB and LoBOX, we outline how interpretability-first models can underpin private assurance pipelines and role-calibrated transparency frameworks. This reframing situates interpretability as infrastructure for private AI governance bridging the gap between technical reliability and institutional accountability.

papers.title: Do Vision Transformers See Like Convolutional Neural Networks?
papers.research_question: How are Vision Transformers solving image tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds key representational differences between Vision Transformers (ViTs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), showing ViTs have more uniform layer representations, incorporate global information earlier via self-attention, and have stronger skip connections that propagate features differently.
papers.conclusion: ViTs and CNNs have clear differences in features and internal structure, with ViTs using global features early and strong skip connections, while local information aggregation is learned from scratch at scale. ViTs show strong spatial localization, promising for future uses like object detection.
papers.key_findings:
ViTs have a more uniform internal representation structure with greater similarity between lower and higher layers compared to the staged similarity in ResNets.
ViTs incorporate global information in lower layers through self-attention, while CNNs are restricted to local receptive fields; this leads to quantitatively different features.
Skip connections in ViTs are more influential than in ResNets, with a phase transition: early layers strongly propagate the CLS token, while later layers propagate spatial token representations.
ViTs preserve input spatial information more faithfully than ResNets in higher layers, especially when trained with a CLS token rather than global average pooling.
Large-scale pretraining data is crucial for ViTs to learn to attend locally in early layers and to develop high-quality intermediate representations for transfer learning.
papers.limitation: The study uses CKA, which summarizes measurements into a single scalar; while complemented with interventional tests and linear probes, more fine-grained methods may reveal additional insights.
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have so far been the de-facto model for visual data. Recent work has shown that (Vision) Transformer models (ViT) can achieve comparable or even superior performance on image classification tasks. This raises a central question: how are Vision Transformers solving these tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations? Analyzing the internal representation structure of ViTs and CNNs on image classification benchmarks, we find striking differences between the two architectures, such as ViT having more uniform representations across all layers. We explore how these differences arise, finding crucial roles played by self-attention, which enables early aggregation of global information, and ViT residual connections, which strongly propagate features from lower to higher layers. We study the ramifications for spatial localization, demonstrating ViTs successfully preserve input spatial information, with noticeable effects from different classification methods. Finally, we study the effect of (pretraining) dataset scale on intermediate features and transfer learning, and conclude with a discussion on connections to new architectures such as the MLP-Mixer.

papers.title: Circuits, Features, and Heuristics in Molecular Transformers
papers.research_question: How do autoregressive transformers trained on drug-like molecules capture the rules of molecular representation and maintain syntactic and chemical validity during generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a mechanistic analysis of an autoregressive transformer trained on drug-like molecules, identifying specialized circuits for syntactic and chemical validity and using sparse autoencoders to extract chemically meaningful features that enhance downstream predictive performance.
papers.conclusion: Molecular transformers develop specialized mechanisms for maintaining syntactic and chemical validity, and sparse autoencoders can disentangle these representations into interpretable features that are useful for downstream tasks and controllable generation.
papers.key_findings:
Identification of attention heads that implement ring and branch syntax circuits, with a division of labor between pointer and writer heads for ring closure.
Discovery of a linearly decodable valence capacity representation in the residual stream that can be steered to modulate bond predictions.
Extraction of sparse feature dictionaries via SAEs that align with chemically meaningful substructures, enabled by an automated fragment-screening pipeline.
Demonstration that SAE-derived features improve transformer embeddings on property prediction tasks, competitive with traditional fingerprints.
SAE features can be used for steering generation towards desired chemical structures.
papers.limitation: Steering with SAE features can degrade validity for complex targets and the effects are not uniform, indicating that SAE latents are preliminary control knobs rather than fully-fledged conditional generators.
papers.abstract: Transformers generate valid and diverse chemical structures, but little is known about the mechanisms that enable these models to capture the rules of molecular representation. We present a mechanistic analysis of autoregressive transformers trained on drug-like small molecules to reveal the computational structure underlying their capabilities across multiple levels of abstraction. We identify computational patterns consistent with low-level syntactic parsing and more abstract chemical validity constraints. Using sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we extract feature dictionaries associated with chemically relevant activation patterns. We validate our findings on downstream tasks and find that mechanistic insights can translate to predictive performance in various practical settings.

papers.title: Inferring gene regulatory network from single-cell transcriptomes with graph autoencoder model
papers.abstract: The gene regulatory structure of cells involves not only the regulatory relationship between two genes, but also the cooperative associations of multiple genes. However, most gene regulatory network inference methods for single cell only focus on and infer the regulatory relationships of pairs of genes, ignoring the global regulatory structure which is crucial to identify the regulations in the complex biological systems. Here, we proposed a graph-based Deep learning model for Regulatory networks Inference among Genes (DeepRIG) from single-cell RNA-seq data. To learn the global regulatory structure, DeepRIG builds a prior regulatory graph by transforming the gene expression of data into the co-expression mode. Then it utilizes a graph autoencoder model to embed the global regulatory information contained in the graph into gene latent embeddings and to reconstruct the gene regulatory network. Extensive benchmarking results demonstrate that DeepRIG can accurately reconstruct the gene regulatory networks and outperform existing methods on multiple simulated networks and real-cell regulatory networks. Additionally, we applied DeepRIG to the samples of human peripheral blood mononuclear cells and triple-negative breast cancer, and presented that DeepRIG can provide accurate cell-type-specific gene regulatory networks inference and identify novel regulators of progression and inhibition.

papers.title: Gene Regulatory Network Inference from Pre-trained Single-Cell Transcriptomics Transformer with Joint Graph Learning
papers.abstract: Inferring gene regulatory networks (GRNs) from single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data is a complex challenge that requires capturing the intricate relationships between genes and their regulatory interactions. In this study, we tackle this challenge by leveraging the single-cell BERT-based pre-trained transformer model (scBERT), trained on extensive unlabeled scRNA-seq data, to augment structured biological knowledge from existing GRNs. We introduce a novel joint graph learning approach that combines the rich contextual representations learned by pre-trained single-cell language models with the structured knowledge encoded in GRNs using graph neural networks (GNNs). By integrating these two modalities, our approach effectively reasons over boththe gene expression level constraints provided by the scRNA-seq data and the structured biological knowledge inherent in GRNs. We evaluate our method on human cell benchmark datasets from the BEELINE study with cell type-specific ground truth networks. The results demonstrate superior performance over current state-of-the-art baselines, offering a deeper understanding of cellular regulatory mechanisms.

papers.title: A Variational Inference Approach to Single-Cell Gene Regulatory Network Inference using Probabilistic Matrix Factorization
papers.abstract: Abstract Inferring gene regulatory networks (GRNs) from single cell data is challenging due to heuristic limitations and a lack of uncertainty estimates in existing methods.
